title: All Nodes at Distance k

concept.title: Give every node a link to its parent, then search outwards
body: The distance between two nodes is the number of edges on the road between them. The nodes at distance `k` from a **target** node can be below it (in its subtree), but also above it or in other branches, reached by going **up** to the parent first. A tree node only knows its children, so first record the **parent** of every node. Then the tree is an ordinary graph where each node has up to three neighbours (two children and the parent).

A breadth-first search from the target, one layer at a time, finds the nodes at distance exactly `k`: after `k` rounds, the nodes in the queue are the answer. A set of visited nodes prevents going back to the node we came from.

This "turn the tree into a graph with parent links" step is useful whenever a question needs to move upwards. The values are printed in increasing order. If no node is at distance `k` (the layer becomes empty), print `-1`.

statement: All values of a binary tree are different. Given the value `target` of a node and a number `k`, print the values of all nodes whose distance from the `target` node is exactly `k` (the distance is the number of edges on the road between two nodes; the road may go up and down). Print the values in increasing order on one line separated by spaces, or `-1` if there is no such node.
inputFormat: The first line has `t`, the number of words in the description of the tree.
The second line has the tree in level order: the root first, then the children of the nodes row by row from left to right. `N` stands for a missing child. There is no `N` at the end.
outputFormat: The values in increasing order on one line, or `-1`.
constraints: The height of the tree is at most 800.
`target` is the value of a node of the tree.

examples.note: The nodes 7 and 4 (below 2) and 1 (up to 3, then down to 1) are at distance 2 from 5.

hints: A tree node cannot reach its parent: record the parent of each node first.
Search from the target layer by layer, moving to the children and to the parent.
Remember the visited nodes so that the search does not turn back.

starter.python:
import sys
input = sys.stdin.readline

class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, val, left=None, right=None):
        self.val = val
        self.left = left
        self.right = right


# Builds a binary tree from a level-order list of words; "N" marks a missing child.
def build_tree(vals):
    if not vals or vals[0] == "N":
        return None
    root = TreeNode(int(vals[0]))
    queue = [root]
    head = 0
    i = 1
    while head < len(queue) and i < len(vals):
        node = queue[head]
        head += 1
        if vals[i] != "N":
            node.left = TreeNode(int(vals[i]))
            queue.append(node.left)
        i += 1
        if i < len(vals) and vals[i] != "N":
            node.right = TreeNode(int(vals[i]))
            queue.append(node.right)
        i += 1
    return root


# Prints a tree in the same level-order form ("empty" for no tree).
def print_tree(root):
    if root is None:
        print("empty")
        return
    out = []
    queue = [root]
    head = 0
    while head < len(queue):
        node = queue[head]
        head += 1
        if node is None:
            out.append("N")
        else:
            out.append(str(node.val))
            queue.append(node.left)
            queue.append(node.right)
    while out and out[-1] == "N":
        out.pop()
    print(" ".join(out))

t = int(input())
vals = input().split()
target, k = map(int, input().split())

answer = at_distance(build_tree(vals), target, k)
print(*answer if answer else [-1])

explanation: A walk records the parent of every node. A breadth-first search from the target, over children and parent links with a visited set, runs for k rounds; the nodes left in the layer are at distance k.
